[SAMIN-DURR:107:2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The fa of fadhālika can answer an implied condition such as if you reflect or seek to know the person.
[SAMIN-DURR:107:2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Alternatively, it coordinates fadhālika with alladhi yukadhdhib; the answer to arayta is omitted, and the question asks whether denial, harming orphans, and neglecting the poor is commendable.
[SAMIN-DURR:107:2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Under the first parse the demonstrative is nominative, either as subject with the relative as predicate or as the predicate of an omitted subject with the relative as modifier; under the second it is accusative by coordination.
[SAMIN-DURR:107:2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · the Shaykh | rejects | The Shaykh rejects accusative coordination as syntactically strange: the natural reading is a new nominative subject, while accusative requires repeating the verb and demonstrative awkwardly points to the prior object.
[SAMIN-DURR:107:2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · the Shaykh | rejects | He says fadhālika refers to the single denier, so it cannot coordinate one entity with another; the omitted answer to arayta is its second object, not an answer.
[SAMIN-DURR:107:2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · the Shaykh | rejects | He objects that hamza does not enter upon naʿma or biʾsa because they are performative rather than declarative.
[SAMIN-DURR:107:2/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The author answers that an interrogative context makes explaining the object of inquiry natural, unlike the Shaykh's example without a question.
[SAMIN-DURR:107:2/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The demonstrative can point forward to the person described after it rather than back to the denier, as in an imperative followed by a description.
[SAMIN-DURR:107:2/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The author replies that this is a response to the preceding interrogative, as grammarians call it, rather than an ordinary declarative answer.

[BIQAI:107:2/r1] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The generic denier may hide his disbelief, but signs growing from its root expose him.
[BIQAI:107:2/r2] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Yaduʿʿ means to shove violently and cruelly; the person wrongs the orphan and does not urge others to honor him.
[BIQAI:107:2/r3] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | God has removed mercy from such a person's heart, a mark of wretchedness; fear of God is the only motive for kindness, so denying requital hardens him.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#2/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو جعفر بن الزبير | reports | He notes that people affiliated with Islam may push an orphan from his rights or fail to care for him, discourage feeding the poor, neglect prayer, show off, and withhold zakat or necessities.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#2/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · أبو جعفر بن الزبير | reports | He reads these traits as those of a denier who expects no judgment, while observing that such acts can occur among Muslims without every person who commits them necessarily being a denier.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#2/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The author compares this trait-based description to hadiths that call one with four specified traits a pure hypocrite and say a fornicator is not a believer while committing the act.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p541/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-Māʿūn is also called al-Dīn, Araʾayta and al-Takdhīb; its central warning is that denial of resurrection and recompense is the root of vices and contempt for sacred matters.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p542/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Harshness to orphans, failure to encourage feeding the poor, neglect of prayer, ostentation and withholding help all mark denial of judgment; belief instead produces praised conduct, so believers must avoid these traits.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p542/r10] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | By rhetorical omission, the shove in the first clause implies contempt in the second, while the urging in the second implies corresponding encouragement in the first; together they signal denial through injury to the weak and neglect of kindness.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p542/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Shoving an orphan reflects the arrogance that destroyed the people of the elephant; neglecting food for the poor reflects the miser's belief that his wealth will make him immortal. | mentions 105:1, 104:3
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p542/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The demonstrative refers to the hateful person far removed from good, who violently shoves and wrongs the orphan because God has removed mercy from his heart; only a wretched person loses that mercy.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p542/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet's supplication asks God for good deeds, avoidance of wrongs, and love of the poor, illustrating the virtue of compassion.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p542/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Mercy toward the weak signals goodness, harshness signals evil, and a person miserly with kind words is even less likely to give from his wealth.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-Anfal 8:4 describes true believers as those who establish prayer and spend from God's provision, connecting with al-Ma'un's themes of prayer and giving. | mentions 8:4

[ALUSI:107:2/r1] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | One view makes the fāʾ causal, following the preceding inducement to discover the denier.
[ALUSI:107:2/r2] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another analysis supplies an omitted condition: if you do not know the denier of recompense or Islam, he is the one who violently pushes the orphan.
[ALUSI:107:2/r3] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Yaduʿʿ means to drive the orphan away violently and rebuke him badly.
[ALUSI:107:2/r4] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | The demonstrative replaces a pronoun to belittle the person, or to signal the reason for the judgment.
[ALUSI:107:2/r5] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The relative construction signals that the attached description is established and certain.
[ALUSI:107:2/r6] ALUSI, d. 1270 · علي والحسن وأبو رجاء واليماني | reports | ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ, and al-Yamānī read yaduʿ with a light dāl: he abandons the orphan, shows no kindness, and shuns him.
[ALUSI:107:7/r13] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | One identifies the denier as Abū Jahl, who supposedly pushed away an orphan under his guardianship when the child asked him for his own property.

[ALUSI:107:7/r15] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Other identifications name al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, ʿAmr ibn ʿĀʾid, or a miserly hypocrite.
[ALUSI:107:7/r17] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī says the sūra's main concern is denial of religion, using orphan-abuse as its identifying sign and the later vices to press the question whether such conduct is good or evil, like the rebuke in 5:91. | mentions 5:91
[ALUSI:107:7/r21] ALUSI, d. 1270 · أبو حيان | reports | Abū Ḥayyān objects that causal coordination making both clauses one group yields an awkward construction; the demonstrative is unnecessary and less natural than a relative clause or direct coordination.
[ALUSI:107:7/r22] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another view treats the demonstrative as an emphatic insertion pointing to the person's extreme distance in evil and corruption.
[ALUSI:107:7/r23] ALUSI, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | A further analysis coordinates two entities and asks whether the deniers and orphan-pushers are in a good or bad state; al-Kashf objects that the pronoun cannot naturally refer to both groups and be replaced by worshippers.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p242/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | The fāʾ may mark causation: the following description results from the suspense created by the opening question.

[ALUSI-FULL:v30p242/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The denier violently pushes the orphan away and rebukes him harshly.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p242/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The demonstrative in place of a pronoun signals contempt and may also indicate the reason for the judgment; the relative clause confirms the trait.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p242/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · علي | reports | Ali, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', and al-Yamani read the verb lightly, meaning that the person abandons, neglects, and shuns the orphan.
[ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The imperfect verbs indicate habitual conduct; the surrounding context condemns people who, despite rescue from hunger and fear, fail their duties of worship and mutual care for orphans and the hungry. | mentions 106:4
[ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Rejecting the orphan and ignoring the poor are habitual traits of those who deny religion; once faith is denied, such cruelty is unsurprising, while its appearance among the devout is more astonishing.
[ELMALILI:107:2-7#3/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Religious pretenders who neglect prayer, show off, and withhold even small help are more astonishingly blameworthy than disbelievers who deny religion and mistreat orphans and the poor.
[ELMALILI:107:2-7#3/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Sūrat al-Māʿūn explains the preceding Sūrat Quraysh; its wording 'woe' and its meaning of withholding aid then connect it to Sūrat al-Humaza. | mentions 106:1, 104:1
[ELMALILI:107:2-7#3/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | After the address to the Prophet to see and understand, Sūrat al-Kawthar condenses the preceding suras, especially those from al-Ḍuḥā, as a final account of Muhammad's rank. | mentions 93:1
[ELMALILI:107:2-7/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The opening fa links this description causally or as the answer to an omitted condition; the definite predicate restricts the referent to people who deny judgment.
[ELMALILI:107:2-7/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The denier of judgment harshly shoves and drives away the orphan, exploiting the child's weakness without mercy or fear of God.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:1/r1] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | prefers | Reports differ on dating: some call the whole surah Meccan, while others call its first three verses Meccan and the rest Medinan; Qutb calls the mixed account likelier.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:1/r2] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Although Qutb leans toward a wholly Medinan setting because hypocrisy and ostentation were unfamiliar in Mecca, he allows later verses to have been appended for thematic continuity.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:1/r3] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | The seven short verses overturn conventional ideas of faith and disbelief and reveal the creed’s mercy and immense good for humanity.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:1/r4] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Religion is not outward forms or ritual; worship matters only when sincere devotion produces good deeds and sound social conduct.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:1/r5] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Religion is an integrated way of life whose worship, rites, and personal and social duties purify hearts and lead people to cooperation, care, and flourishing.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:1/r6] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | A verbal claim to Islam and performance of prayer or other rites do not prove faith; its signs must appear in the person’s conduct.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:1/r7] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Faith, once settled in the heart, immediately moves a person to righteous action; failure to move shows that faith is absent.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:1/r8] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | The opening question summons anyone able to see to identify the person who denies the Judgment.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:2/r1] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | The Qur’an answers who denies the Judgment by pointing to the person who shoves the orphan and refuses care for the poor, surprising under conventional definitions of faith.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:2/r2] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | The verb describes forcefully pushing the orphan, humiliating and harming the child.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:3/r2] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | If belief were genuine, the person would neither push the orphan away nor neglect urging food for the poor.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:3/r3] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | True assent transforms the heart and prompts kindness and care for fellow humans who need protection.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:3/r4] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | God asks for deeds that confirm words; words without confirming action are worthless before Him.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:3/r5] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | These opening verses state with unusual clarity the spirit of the creed and the nature of the religion.
[QUTB-ZILAL:107:3/r6] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Qutb declines to debate juristic boundaries of faith and Islam: those govern legal transactions, while this surah states God’s measure of the underlying reality.

[CORPUSCORANICUM:107:1-3:kommentar/r1] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | holds | The sura systematically links religious beliefs and ritual actions with an individual’s moral conduct in daily life.

[CORPUSCORANICUM:107:2-3:anmerkung/r3] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | holds | The orphan and widow and the poor and wretched are stereotyped pairings in the Hebrew Bible, with examples in Exodus, Deuteronomy, Malachi, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel.

[CORPUSCORANICUM:107:2-3:anmerkung/r5] CORPUSCORANICUM · author | reports | The notes also refer readers to related material on 93:9, 90:11–16, and the prophetic-ethical command to give full measure in 83:1–4. | mentions 93:9, 90:11, 90:12, 90:13, 90:14, 90:15, 90:16, 83:1, 83:2, 83:3, 83:4
